title: The 5 Highest-Flying Birds, Ranked (#1 Hit a Jet at 37,000 Feet)

scenes.text: The five highest flying birds, ranked. Number one met a passenger jet at cruising height.

scenes.label: Alpine chough · 26,000 ft
scenes.text: Number five: the alpine chough. About 26,000 feet, recorded high on Mount Everest, where it follows climbers.

scenes.label: Whooper swan · 27,000 ft
scenes.text: Number four: the whooper swan. 27,000 feet. In 1967 a pilot spotted a flock over the Hebrides, and radar confirmed it.

scenes.label: Bar-headed goose · 29,000 ft
scenes.text: Number three: the bar-headed goose. Around 29,000 feet, straight over the Himalayas, twice a year.

scenes.label: Common crane · 33,000 ft
scenes.text: Number two: the common crane. About 33,000 feet over the Himalayas. That is airliner height.

scenes.label: Rüppell's vulture · 37,000 ft
scenes.text: Number one: Rüppell's vulture. 37,000 feet. In 1973 one flew into a jet engine over Ivory Coast, and the plane still landed.

description:
The five highest-flying birds ever recorded, ranked by maximum altitude.
The alpine chough reaches about 26,000 feet on Everest, the whooper swan was tracked at 27,000 feet by radar in 1967, the bar-headed goose crosses the Himalayas at around 29,000 feet, and the common crane has been reported at about 33,000 feet. Number one is Rüppell's vulture: in 1973 one was sucked into an airliner's engine at 37,000 feet over Ivory Coast, and the plane landed safely.
Which of these surprised you most?
first_comment: At 37,000 feet there is about a quarter of the oxygen at sea level, and most of these birds barely notice. Who would you have put at number one, and what should we rank next?
